hehe, ele não pode mandar a sugestão de código de como seria sem o problema?

Imagina a pessoa que está começando a contribuir com o MAME? Ela desanima
Ainda mais que esse processo de code review como tem sido feito é demorado

Se você manda uma contribuição pequena, não está boa porque está "incompleta" (mesmo podendo ser incrementada com PR subsequentes).

Se manda uma contribuição completa, fica meses parada no code review e para descobrir que um monte de coisa que fez "não era boa o bastante" e que muito tempo acabou sendo perdido.

O que é o certo a se fazer então? 🤔

Eu tinha um pull request de 3 anos de idade que ainda não tinha sido aceito. Mês passado abri um PR novo com um pedacinho pequeno do PR maior e depois de passar por code-review e ajustes finalmente foi aceito.

Aí teve um release do MAME alguns dias atrás como meu driver pela metade, sendo que eu tenho um driver muito melhorado sentado no meu HD (e também naquele PR de 3 anos atrás)

Eu fechei o PR antigo, fiz git squase de tudo num commit só, fiz rebase, pra tirar do commit aquele pedacinho que já entrou nesse release, e submeti como um PR novo.

Já veio o review dizendo que "continua errado"

Aí eu percebi que uma das coisas que o Cuavas diz que tá "errado" é idêntico ao estilo de código usado nos cores das outras variantes do TOSHIBA TLCS-900 que já estão há uns 4 ou 5 anos assim no MAME. E eu tinha simplesmente feito meu código seguindo o mesmo estilo.

Fiz a pergunta sobre isso, mas até agora não ouvi nenhuma resposta. Me dá a sensação de que eu estou sendo ignorado.

webpage.author: David Cassel

text.text: Steve Wozniak Reunites With the Historic Homebrew Computer Club
When they met in 1975, the Homebrew Computer Club had no idea that they'd see the fulfillment of their deepest wish: a world with computers for everyone.

texts.text: “The 5th of March was a rainy night in Silicon Valley,” wrote Steven Levy. The year was 1975, and dozens sat on the cement floor of

text.text: Gordon French

texts.text: ‘s garage, awaiting the historic first meeting of the Homebrew Computer Club.

text.text: In that long-ago world where personal computers didn’t exist, each of them had answered the call of an announcement asking if they were already building their own — or at least an input-output device, “or some other digital black magic box” — and invited them all to “a gathering of people with likeminded interests.”
“Exchange information, swap ideas, help work on a project, whatever …”

texts.text: In his book, “

text.text: H
ackers:
Heroes of the Computer Revolution

texts.text: ,” Levy writes that “it turned out that six of the thirty-two had built their own computer system of some sort,” and they became one of the most influential groups in the history of technology. The chapter notes that a shy 24-year-old

text.text: Steve Wozniak

texts.text: was “dragged along” to the meeting by his friend Alan Baum, a fellow HP engineer.
Nearly half a century later — most of a lifetime — 10 of them reunited for a

text.text: special
event

texts.text: on

text.text: Zoom

texts.text: . Steve Wozniak, now 75, remembered being a shy twentysomething who “never once raised my hand to speak.”

text.text: But Wozniak also remembered — they all very clearly remembered — what happened next: how they’d realized a shared dream of changing the world.
“I Want To Be Part of This”

texts.text: The interview took place on

text.text: a YouTube channel

texts.text: hosted by

text.text: John Draper

texts.text: , who in 1974 was a

text.text: legendary phone phreak

texts.text: — while still living at home with his parents. Wozniak had been using a TV as an output device for videogames — when he’d heard John Draper’s tales of connecting a teletype with an acoustic modem to a computer on the other side of the country using ARPAnet.

“When I saw that, I said ‘Oh my god, I want to be a part of this,” Woz remembered on the call. So he’d copied a modem schematic, bought a teletype keyboard, and jury-rigged his own connection across the continent-spanning

text.text: ARPAnet

texts.text: . “And that was a real big hot thing in my life.”

text.text: But soon another club meeting had ended with a datasheet for an upcoming 8-bit microprocessor — which inspired Wozniak on a far-reaching path. Why cross the country to reach a computer if you already had your own microprocessor right here at home?

Wozniak thought, “This is how I turn my little terminal, talking to far-away TVs, into a real computer.” Wozniak couldn’t afford the latest Intel processors, but as a design engineer at HP, he could get a discount on processors — which led him to realize a dream he’d had for years. “I now had a formula to own my own computer — and it worked.”
“I just listened, and it was like the most incredible science fiction you ever heard. And I was just totally inspired by it.”
—Steve Wozniak

You can hear the excitement in Wozniak’s voice as he remembers what happened next. HP had a single computer that 40 people were sharing. But now, “I had this little tiny computer with my own TV set, sitting on my desk at Hewlett-Packard, and I could type in my own programs and come up with solutions … I was just having the time of my life!”

texts.text: Wozniak, of course, would go on to build Apple’s

text.text: first personal computers

texts.text: , which helped Apple become the

text.text: most profitable company on earth

texts.text: . But Wozniak closes by saying the Homebrew Computer Club “was the heart of it all. It’s what turned me on to the fact that people were interested in things like computers we could afford.”

text.text: At the club, speakers from top local universities like Stanford and Berkeley would “talk about how it was going to change life totally,” Woz remembered — saying again that he didn’t speak. “I just listened, and it was like the most incredible science fiction you ever heard. And I was just totally inspired by it. All of a sudden, the geek was going to be important, and education was going to be better. And communication — being able to send messages to a lot of people to organize things quickly.”

Some of them were high school students — but the impact was there, Wozniak says, partly from having such good friends. “That was a real big motivating factor. That was so important. Why would I go on and try to do bigger things, start a company even — why would I do that if I didn’t have people around me saying, ‘What you’re doing’s good.'”

texts.text: And Woz says when Apple went public, he gave tens of millions of his

text.text: Apple stock

texts.text: to early Apple employees who’d come from the Homebrew Computer Club. “I just felt they deserved it as much as I did. Because that was really where all my inspiration came from.”

text.text: And he would also fly into computer clubs around the U.S., “because I wanted to tell them where Apple came from, where I came from: It was the Homebrew Computer Club.
“And having clubs is that important — you know, associating with others and sharing ideas and collaborating, that sort of thing. That was very important to me to get that message out.”
“It Was Really the People”

texts.text: Electrical engineer

text.text: Lee Felsenstein

texts.text: spoke about the club’s founding, and in

text.text: the second part

texts.text: , he remembered how Wozniak “staked out the only seat in the whole auditorium with a power outlet.”
Draper jumped in to remember Woz typing in assembly code for his

text.text: homegrown interpreter for the BASIC programming language

texts.text: — and got it up and running “… until somebody unplugged the computer. But he got enough of it running to really give a killer demonstration.”

text.text: Wozniak grinned and nodded, but quickly emphasized: “Less than the technology that came out of the club … It was really the people like Lee that had done good things … All the people in the club, that were so good in their hearts towards the purpose of what technology could do for us, was much more important than how to do it and which parts are better and which parts accomplish the job … And that really was more my inspiration.”
Woz also said that “I wanted computers for the normal people. I’d wanted it for years and years before that, almost a decade.”

texts.text: Soon they were reminiscing about the old times — not all of it legal. Original club member Dan Sokol also remembered building his own blue box to sneak free long-distance phone calls from the phone company, just like

text.text: John Draper

texts.text: — only to discover it didn’t work. So, “Woz showed up with John, John picked up the box, pushed each of the buttons, and said ‘Oh, your frequencies are off!’ and then tuned it by ear — and it worked after that.”

text.text: Another club member on the call also remembered building his own blue boxes — and how struggling musicians had figured out how to mimic the 2600 tone to get their own free long-distance phone calls.

Later in the call, Draper remembered working at Apple as employee #13 — and finishing up his telephone-interfacing “Charlie Board” (which, among other things, could mimic toll-free phone lines). Draper left instructions for Wozniak on how to use it, “And you programmed it to call Steve Jobs’ home — over and over and over again!”
Draper adds that the next day, Steve Jobs came in, “just madder than a wet hen.”

But then later, at a big east-coast party for phone phreaks, one of the guests reprogrammed Draper’s device into a full-fledged, free-phone-call blue box. Draper says his phone line was being “heavily monitored” at this time. “A few hours later, the Pennsylvania state troopers came with two helicopters and 17 state troopers … It was crazy.”

Estou aqui refletindo que faz mais de 25 anos que alguém inventou um cabo de porta paralela fora do padrão. A placa é rara, mas eu tenho uma (e não conheço ninguém mais que tenha uma placa dessas, e não acho pra comprar outra dessas em lugar nenhum). O cabo eu não tenho, e nem acho pra comprar, e não sei dizer como é o cabo (não achei nenhuma documentação).

Mas eu tenho o software das duas pontas: de um lado o firmware da placa e do outro o programa de Windows. Levantando o esquemático a partir da placa que tenho em mãos, sei qual é a cara do cabo do lado de cá, já mapeei todos os sinais da PPI nos pinos do conector DB-15 (macho no cabo). E inspecionando o disasm da DLL (e também o firmware da placa) estou aos pouquinhos entendendo qual é a cara da outra ponta do cabo.

É incrível que a única coisa que eu não tenho é um amontoado de fios de um cabo peculiar, e que com o resto provavelmente vou conseguir documentar como esse cabo é. Sem nunca pegar ele nas mãos. É, DE FATO arqueologia digital!
só é arqueologia de verdade se um europeu roubar e levar para um museu

Inspecionando um disasm do arquivo ppkn50.dll usado pelo programa de Windows HD-TechManager5000, estou conseguindo começar a inferir como funciona o protocolo de comunicação com a placa HDAE5000. Existem algumas funções fornecidas pela DLL que quando executadas chamam a função 0x10002810 com um valor numérico passado pela pilha. Eu acho que esse valor numérico deve também ser enviado via porta paralela para identificar a operação requisitada. Segue abaixo uma tabela dos valores numéricos e respectivas funções:

    0x01: Test The KN PP
    0x02: Escape Keyboard To Play
    0x03: Read Fsb From Kn Hd To Kn Mem
    0x04: Send Fsb From Kn Mem To PC
    0x05: Send Fsb From PC To Kn Mem
    0x06: Write Fsb From Kn Mem To Kn Hd / Send Several File Direct To KN HD
    0x07: Load File From Kn Hd To Kn Mem
    0x08: Load File From Kn Hd To PC
    0x09: Load File From Kn Hd Direct To PC
    0x0A: Send File From PC To KN Mem / Send File From PC To KN HD
    0x0B: Save File From KN Mem To KN Hd
    0x0D: Save File From PC Direct To KN Hd / Save PC Mem Direct To KN Hd
    0x0E: Test Song Info From Kn Hd
    0x10: Delete File On Kn Hd
    0x11: Format The Kn 50 Hard Disk
    0x12: Turn Off The Kn 50 Hd Motor
Parece mais alto nível do que eu imaginaria

o endereço 0xFFFFE8 é ROM e tem o valor 0x0A

aí eu troquei as ROMs e lugar no emulador e bootei com debugger e, de fato, tem um vetor de interrupções nas ROMs "table_data" e tem um código parecido no vetor de RESET
E no par de table_data ROMs tem 0xFF naquela posição de memória que a rotina "Get_Firmware_Version" lê
uma teoria que tenho é de que talvez esse seja um mecanismo para desbricar a placa, bootando de uma segunda cópia do mecanismo de update (essa em mask ROM, que não tem como dar erro)
a técnica seria dessoldar os resistores, e soldá-los na outra posição, pra fazer a troca dos sinais de chip-enable das ROMs e acessar esse código de recuperação

mas... tem mais!

vejo que também tem sinais de reset e write-enable nos footprints das mask ROMs. Em pinos "NC" (not connected) que têm a mesma numeração que esses sinais teriam em chips de FLASH ROM.

Então a outra teoria é de que talvez isso seja "órgão vestigial" na PCB, de uma época em que ela estava sendo ainda desenvolvida e que se usava memória flash ali também.
e esses sinais também estão chaveados com resistores, para fazer ligações opcionais

Essa CPU tem uma meia duzia de chip selects para trabalhar com pedaçinhos do memory map

Legalmente, emulação não ilegal, pelo menos não na legislação dos EUA que é o que eles empurram para o resto do mundo

Casos como Sony Computer Entertainment America, Inc. v. Bleem LLC e Sony Computer Entertainment v. Connectix já deram precedentes para a emulação ser considerada legal e fair use, desde que nenhum conteúdo protegido por copyright seja distribuído com os emuladores
Mas recentemente rolou aquela treta com o Yuzu que eles acabaram resolvendo entre eles que abriu precedentes para perseguição à emulação, principalmente em consoles mais recentes
Tem um emulador de PS4, shadPS4, acho o nome, que vem tendo progressos rápidos e a Sony começou a perseguir também

A Sony ainda lucra muito com o PS4 e há rumores até de lançarem um PS4 portátil. O Switch 2 provavelmente vai usar de base a mesma arquitetura do Switch atual que de uma forma ou de outra, já está caminhando para ser o console mais vendido da história
